correct: Sweep shavings from the floor around your bench so that you do not slip.

wrong.text: Rest the plane on its sole so the blade stays ready for use.
wrong.why: That dulls the blade and exposes it. Lay the plane on its side.

wrong.text: Hold the short piece in one hand and plane it against your chest.
wrong.why: The plane can slip into you. Hold the work in the vice or against a stop.

wrong.text: Run your hand along the sole to feel how far the blade projects.
wrong.why: That can cut your fingers. Sight along the sole against the light.

wrong.text: Brush shavings away with your bare palm while the plane is moving.
wrong.why: Hands near the moving blade get cut. Stop first and use a bench brush.

distractors.name: Rip saw
distractors.why: This stock is already sawn near size. The tenon saw squares the ends.

distractors.name: Sash cramp
distractors.why: Nothing is being glued up in this job.

distractors.name: Spokeshave
distractors.why: A spokeshave is for curves. These faces must be flat.

distractors.name: Mortise chisel
distractors.why: No joint is being cut here.

decisions.prompt: The best face is flat and has its face mark. What do you plane next?

options.text: The best edge, square to the face side
options.consequence: Face side and face edge now give two true surfaces to gauge from.

options.text: The opposite face, down to thickness
options.consequence: You have nothing square to gauge from yet, so the thickness will not be even.

options.text: Both ends, to get the length
options.consequence: End grain tears when planed first, and the ends may not be square to a true edge.

decisions.prompt: The plane leaves torn patches on the edge. What do you do?

options.text: Turn the piece and plane with the grain
options.consequence: The shaving now lifts cleanly and the surface comes up smooth.

options.text: Press harder and take a thicker cut
options.consequence: Thicker cuts tear deeper, and you may go past the line.

options.text: Sand the torn patches out now
options.consequence: Grit left on the wood dulls the plane, and the edge goes out of square.

decisions.prompt: You are about to gauge the width. Where does the gauge stock run?

options.text: Against the face edge you have planed
options.consequence: The width line runs true because it follows a true edge.

options.text: Against the rough sawn edge
options.consequence: The line copies every wave of the rough edge, so the width varies.

options.text: Against whichever edge is nearer to you
options.consequence: Working from different edges puts the line out by the difference between them.

observations.prompt: You sight across two winding strips on the face. What shows the face is out of winding?

options.text: The top edges of the strips line up
One strip sits higher at one end
options.why: That shows the face is twisted.

options.text: The strips rock when pressed
options.why: That shows the face is hollow or round.

numerics.prompt: A finished rail is {l} mm long. You allow {a} mm for squaring the ends. What length of sawn stock do you order, in mm?
The finished width is {w} mm. You allow {a} mm on the width for planing. What sawn width do you need, in mm?

faults.scenario: Chidi's rail is thicker at one end than the other, and his marks are hard to find. Here is what he did.

lines.text: He gauged the thickness from the rough face.
lines.why: Gauge only from the planed face side, or the thickness follows the rough face.

lines.text: He kept planing after reaching the gauge line.
lines.why: Going past the line makes that part undersize.

lines.text: He left off the face side and face edge marks.
lines.why: Without marks he cannot tell which surfaces are true.

lines.text: He set the plane for a fine cut near the line.
lines.why: That is the right way to finish to a line.

lines.text: He laid the plane on its side between cuts.

written.explainPrompt: Why are the face side and face edge prepared first, and all other work measured from them?
written.explainGuide: They are the true reference surfaces. Gauging and squaring from them keeps every other line parallel and square, so the piece comes out even.

correct: Lift the saw clear before moving the board on the trestles.

wrong.text: Kneel on the board to hold it while a friend supports the free end by hand near the saw.
wrong.why: A hand near the saw path gets cut. Support it away from the cut or on trestles.

wrong.text: Leave the saw standing in the cut when you stop for a break.
wrong.why: It can fall or be knocked. Lay it safely on the bench.

wrong.text: Saw hard and fast at the start so the blade bites.
wrong.why: The saw jumps out of a forced start. Start with light strokes.

distractors.name: Jack plane
distractors.why: Planing comes later. This job is about sawing.

distractors.name: Coping saw
distractors.why: A coping saw cuts curves, not long straight cuts.

distractors.name: Bevel-edged chisel
distractors.why: No waste is chopped out here.

distractors.name: Mallet
distractors.why: Nothing here is struck.

decisions.prompt: You must cut along the grain of a long board. Which saw do you use?

options.text: The rip saw
options.consequence: Its chisel-shaped teeth chop along the grain and clear fast.

options.text: The cross-cut saw
options.consequence: Its knife-point teeth score across the grain, so along the grain they clog and cut slowly.

options.text: The tenon saw
options.consequence: Its fine teeth clog at once, and the blade is far too short for this cut.

decisions.prompt: Halfway along the rip, the saw starts to bind. What do you do?

options.text: Stop, and open the kerf with a small wedge
options.consequence: The saw runs free again and the cut stays straight.

options.text: Push harder to force it through to the far end
options.consequence: Forcing buckles the blade and the cut wanders off the line.

options.text: Twist the handle to widen the cut
options.consequence: Twisting bends the blade and can spoil the saw set.

decisions.prompt: You are nearly through a cross-cut, and the off-cut is heavy. What do you do?

options.text: Support the off-cut and finish with light strokes
options.consequence: The cut ends cleanly with no splitting.

options.text: Saw faster so it drops away cleanly
options.consequence: It drops early and tears a long split from the board.

options.text: Let it fall and trim the split later with a sharp plane
options.consequence: The split runs into the good timber, and the piece is short.

observations.prompt: After sawing, where should the pencil or knife line be?

options.text: Still visible on the piece you are keeping
Gone, cut away by the saw as it passed along
options.why: The kerf has eaten into the piece, so it is undersize.

options.text: A full 10 mm from the cut
options.why: That leaves far too much cleaning up.

numerics.prompt: A board takes {c} cross-cuts, with a {k} mm kerf at each. What is the total length lost to the saw, in mm?

faults.scenario: Amaka's shelf board came out 2 mm short, and its end has a split. Here is what she did.

lines.text: She sawed straight down the middle of the line.
lines.why: The kerf took half its width from the keep side.

lines.text: She let the off-cut hang unsupported near the end.
lines.why: Its weight tore a split into the board.

lines.text: She forced the saw on the last few strokes.
lines.why: Forcing wanders the cut and splits the end. Let the teeth work.

lines.text: She used the full length of the blade.
She marked the cross-cut line with a knife.

written.explainPrompt: Why does a rip saw cut along the grain better than a cross-cut saw?
written.explainGuide: Rip saw teeth are chisel-shaped and chop the fibres end-on along the grain. Cross-cut teeth are knife-pointed and are made to sever fibres across the grain.

correct: Keep the mallet head clear of your other hand when chopping.

wrong.text: Hold the rail in one hand while you chop the mortise with the other.
wrong.why: The chisel can skid. Cramp the work to the bench.

wrong.text: Chop over the bench vice jaw so the blows ring through.
wrong.why: Hollow support makes it bounce. Chop over a solid part of the bench.

wrong.text: Lever waste out with the chisel held towards your stomach.
wrong.why: A slip drives it into you. Keep the edge pointing away.

distractors.name: Marking gauge with a single pin
distractors.why: A mortise needs two lines at once: use the mortise gauge.

distractors.name: Rip saw
distractors.why: Too coarse: use the tenon saw for cheeks and shoulders.

distractors.name: Claw hammer
distractors.why: It splits a chisel handle. Use the mallet.

distractors.name: Coping saw
distractors.why: This joint has straight cuts only.

decisions.prompt: Stock is 25 mm thick. How do you set the mortise gauge?

options.text: To the width of the mortise chisel
options.consequence: The mortise can be chopped exactly between the lines.

options.text: To half the stock thickness
options.consequence: That leaves weak thin cheeks around a very wide mortise.

options.text: To any width near one-third
options.consequence: No chisel matches the gauge, so the sides of the mortise go ragged.

decisions.prompt: How far do you chop from the first edge?

options.text: Halfway, then turn the piece and meet from the other edge
options.consequence: Both faces stay clean with no split-out.

options.text: Straight through from one side
options.consequence: The far face bursts out as the chisel breaks through.

options.text: Most of the way through, then drill out the rest from below
options.consequence: The drill wanders, and the hole no longer lines up.

decisions.prompt: The tenon needs hard mallet blows to go in. What do you do?

options.text: Pare the tenon cheeks and test again
options.consequence: It now slides in with hand pressure and the shoulders close.

options.text: Drive it home with the mallet anyway
options.consequence: The tight tenon splits the mortised rail.

options.text: Widen the mortise with a coarse rasp
options.consequence: The mortise goes out of parallel and the joint rocks.

observations.prompt: The joint is well cut when:

options.text: The tenon slides in by hand and the shoulders close tight
The tenon rattles a little so that glue can get into the gaps
options.why: Glue cannot fill gaps. A loose joint is a weak joint.

options.text: It needs a heavy hammer to close the shoulders
options.why: That much force splits the mortised piece.

numerics.prompt: Stock is {t} mm thick. By the one-third rule, how thick should the tenon be, in mm?
numerics.working: Tenon ≈ {t} ÷ 3 = {answer} mm (then use the nearest chisel size).

faults.scenario: Bola's frame rail sits out of line, and its tenon is loose. Here is what she did.

lines.text: She gauged the rail from one face and the stile from the other.
lines.why: Any thickness difference pushes the joint out of line. Gauge both from the face side.

lines.text: She chopped the mortise wider than the tenon.
lines.why: The tenon is loose and the joint is weak.

lines.text: She marked the shoulders with a knife.
lines.why: A knife line gives a clean shoulder.

lines.text: She chopped halfway from each edge.
lines.why: That stops the mortise splitting out.

written.explainPrompt: Why is a tenon usually made about one-third of the stock thickness?
written.explainGuide: It leaves enough wood on both cheeks of the mortise to stay strong, while the tenon itself stays thick enough. Thicker weakens the mortised piece; thinner weakens the tenon.

correct: Pass chisels to others handle first.

wrong.text: Hold the board against your thigh while you saw the tails.
wrong.why: A slip cuts your leg. Hold it in the vice.

wrong.text: Chop waste towards your free hand so you can feel the depth.
wrong.why: Hands stay behind the edge. Check depth by eye.

wrong.text: Blow the waste out of the joint with your mouth.
wrong.why: Dust and chips fly into your eyes. Use a small brush.

distractors.name: Rip saw
distractors.why: Far too coarse for fine joint cutting.

distractors.name: Jack plane
distractors.why: The boards are already prepared.

distractors.name: Sash cramp
distractors.why: A box corner is closed by hand pressure and light taps.

distractors.name: Claw hammer
distractors.why: It damages chisel handles and bruises the wood. Use the mallet.

decisions.prompt: You are working in iroko, a hardwood. Which slope do you mark?

options.consequence: A gentle slope suits hardwood, which resists crushing.
That is the softwood slope. It leaves weak short grain at the corners of hard timber.
So steep a slope has short grain that snaps straight off.

decisions.prompt: Your tail lines are clear. Where do you saw?

options.text: Just on the waste side of each line
options.consequence: The lines survive, so the tails keep their exact shape.

options.text: Straight down the middle of each line
options.consequence: The line is gone, and the joint comes out loose by half a saw cut.

options.text: On the tail side, then pare back
options.consequence: The tail is undersize and cannot be recovered: the joint has gaps.

decisions.prompt: The tails are cut. How do you mark the pins?

options.text: Scribe round the tails with a marking knife
options.consequence: The pins are an exact copy of these tails, small errors included.

options.text: Set them out with a rule and the template
options.consequence: They no longer match the tails as actually cut, so gaps appear.

options.text: Draw round the tails with a thick pencil
options.consequence: The thick line sits away from the tail, so the pins come out too small.

observations.prompt: You test-fit the corner. Which result means the joint is good?

options.text: It seats with light taps and no gaps show
It only closes with hard mallet blows
options.why: That force splits the short grain.

options.text: It slides together and falls apart when lifted
options.why: Too loose: glue will not fill those gaps.

numerics.prompt: A tail is {h} mm long, with a 1:6 slope. How far does the slope run sideways over that length, in mm?

faults.scenario: Tunde cut a dovetailed box corner. It shows gaps. Here is what he did.

lines.text: He marked the slopes so that they ran the wrong way, narrowing towards the end of the board.
lines.why: A reversed slope pulls apart instead of locking.

lines.text: He chopped beyond the gauge line on the inside face.
lines.why: The cut shows as a gap when the joint closes.

lines.text: He cut the tails first and transferred them to the pins.
He kept the work in the vice while sawing.

written.explainPrompt: Why are the tails normally cut before the pins?
written.explainGuide: The tails set the shape. Marking the pins directly from them transfers any small error, so the two parts still match and fit.

correct: Keep your hands behind the chisel when paring the housing.

wrong.text: Steady the board with your hand in front of the saw.
wrong.why: A slipping saw goes straight into the hand. Cramp the board.

wrong.text: Hold the router plane by its cutter to guide it.
wrong.why: The cutter is sharp. Use both handles.

wrong.text: Stand the chisel edge-up on the bench to keep it handy.
wrong.why: An exposed edge cuts hands. Lay it flat, away from the edge of the bench.

distractors.name: Mortise gauge
distractors.why: There is no mortise here. The single-pin gauge sets the depth.

distractors.name: Rip saw
distractors.why: The housing is cut across the grain, with a fine saw.

distractors.name: Spokeshave
distractors.why: This job has no curves.

distractors.name: Sash cramp
distractors.why: These joints are test-fitted, not glued in this exercise.

decisions.prompt: How do you mark the width of the housing?

options.text: Lay the shelf itself on the board and mark both sides
options.consequence: The housing is exactly as wide as the shelf you are fitting.

options.text: Measure the shelf with a rule and copy the figure
options.consequence: A rule reading is out by a fraction, so the fit is slack or tight.

options.text: Mark it a little wider so the shelf goes in easily
options.consequence: The shelf rattles, and a gap shows at the front.

decisions.prompt: The board is 18 mm thick. What depth do you gauge?

options.text: About 6 mm, one-third of the thickness
options.consequence: The shelf is well held, and the board stays strong.

options.text: About 12 mm, two-thirds of the thickness
options.consequence: Too little wood is left, and the board can split along the housing.

options.text: About 2 mm, as little as possible
options.consequence: The housing is too shallow to hold the shelf.

decisions.prompt: For a cross-halving, from which face do you mark the depth?

options.text: From the top face of one and the bottom face of the other
options.consequence: The two pieces finish flush on both sides.

options.text: From the top face of both pieces, so they are marked alike
options.consequence: The pieces stand proud of each other and do not finish flush.

options.text: From whichever face is cleanest
options.consequence: Any difference in thickness shows as a step in the joint.

observations.prompt: What shows that the housing is right?

options.text: The shelf slides in by hand with no play
The shelf must be hammered in tightly
options.why: That can split the side.

options.text: The shelf moves up and down in the housing
options.why: That is too wide and will show gaps.

numerics.prompt: A board is {t} mm thick. What is the housing depth at one-third of the thickness, in mm?
Two pieces {t} mm thick are cross-halved. How deep is the cut in each piece, in mm?

faults.scenario: Ngozi's cross-halving has a step in it, and her housing shelf rocks. Here is what she did.

lines.text: She gauged both halving cuts from the top face.
lines.why: The pieces will not finish flush.

lines.text: She checked the housing depth at one end only.
lines.why: The depth can vary along the housing, so check at both ends.

lines.text: She marked the housing width from the shelf itself.
She cramped the board before sawing.

written.explainPrompt: Why is the width of a housing marked from the shelf rather than with a rule?
written.explainGuide: The actual piece gives the exact width, so the joint fits with no play. A rule reading adds small errors.

correct: Keep your fingers clear of the bit when starting the drill.

wrong.text: Hold the board in your lap while drilling the dowel holes.
wrong.why: The bit can run through into you. Clamp the work.

wrong.text: Taste a drop of glue to check if it is still fresh.
wrong.why: Glue is not food. Check its date and pour.

wrong.text: Wipe glue from the cramp bar with your fingers while it is being tightened.
wrong.why: Fingers get nipped. Wait until it is tight, then use a damp cloth.

distractors.name: Tenon saw
distractors.why: Nothing is being cut to length in this job.

distractors.name: Coping saw
distractors.why: This is straight edge work.

distractors.name: Marking knife and bevel
distractors.why: No angled marking is needed.

distractors.name: Mallet and mortise chisel
distractors.why: There are no mortises here.

decisions.prompt: How do you lay out the boards before jointing?

options.text: With the growth rings alternating, board by board
options.consequence: Each board's cupping counters the next, so the panel stays flat.

options.text: All with the heart side up
options.consequence: All the boards cup the same way, and the panel bends.

options.text: Whichever way the colours look best along the panel
options.consequence: Looks alone can leave several boards cupping together.

decisions.prompt: Where do you put the sash cramps?

options.text: Alternately above and below the panel
options.consequence: The forces balance, and the panel stays flat.

options.text: All underneath the panel, where they stay out of the way
options.consequence: The pull is all on one side, and the panel bows.

options.text: One only, at the centre
options.consequence: The ends gape, because no pressure reaches them.

decisions.prompt: The dowels are ready. What comes before the glue?

options.text: A dry run with all the cramps
options.consequence: Any tight dowel or gap shows while it can still be fixed.

options.text: Nothing: go straight to gluing
options.consequence: A problem found once the glue is on cannot be fixed in time.

options.text: Plane the panel flat first
options.consequence: The panel is not assembled yet, so there is nothing to plane.

observations.prompt: How should the finished panel look?

options.text: Flat, with tight, nearly invisible joint lines
With a line of squeezed glue left on the face
options.why: Dried glue blocks the finish. Wipe it off.

options.text: Bowed slightly towards the cramps
options.why: That shows the cramps were all on one side.

numerics.prompt: A dowel is {d} mm in diameter. Using a length of 5 × diameter, how long is each dowel, in mm?
A joint is {l} mm long, with dowels 150 mm apart and one 75 mm from each end. How many dowels are needed?

faults.scenario: Efe's table-top panel came out bowed, with one joint open. Here is what he did.

lines.text: He put all the cramps on one side.
lines.why: That bows the panel. Alternate them.

lines.text: He glued up without a dry run.
lines.why: The bad joint was found too late.

lines.text: He overtightened the cramps until no glue was left in the joint.
He shot the edges straight and square first.

written.explainPrompt: Why are boards arranged with their growth rings alternating?
written.explainGuide: Boards cup as they dry. Alternating the rings makes each board cup the opposite way to the next, which reduces the cupping of the whole panel.

correct: Support the long ends of sash cramps so they cannot tip.

wrong.text: Lean over the frame and hold it down with your chest while tightening.
wrong.why: A slipping cramp can hit you. Rest the frame on bearers.

wrong.text: Leave the cramps sticking out in the walkway overnight.
wrong.why: They are a trip hazard. Set the frame aside out of the way.

wrong.text: Use your hand as a cramp block to protect the wood.
wrong.why: Fingers get crushed. Use scraps.

distractors.name: Tenon saw
distractors.why: The joints are already cut.

distractors.name: Jack plane
distractors.why: Flushing off comes after the glue sets, and it is not the main job here.

distractors.name: Marking gauge
distractors.why: The marking out is finished.

distractors.name: Mortise chisel
distractors.why: The joints are already cut.

decisions.prompt: One diagonal measures 4 mm longer than the other. What do you do?

options.text: Set the cramps slightly skew to pull the long diagonal in
options.consequence: The diagonals come equal, so the frame is square.

options.text: Plane one rail shorter until the two diagonals are the same
options.consequence: The rails were fine: now the frame has a gap.

options.text: Glue it up and fix it later
options.consequence: Once the glue sets, the frame stays out of square.

decisions.prompt: What goes between the cramp jaws and the frame?

options.text: Scrap cramp blocks
options.consequence: The pressure spreads and the face stays unmarked.

options.text: Nothing: the jaws need a firm grip
options.consequence: The jaws bite dents into the finished face.

options.text: A wet cloth folded in two
options.consequence: It compresses unevenly and marks the wood with water.

decisions.prompt: Glue is squeezing from the joints. What do you do?

options.text: Wipe it off now with a damp cloth
options.consequence: The surface stays clean, so the finish takes evenly.

options.text: Leave it to dry and sand it later
options.consequence: Glue that soaks in stops stain and leaves pale patches.

options.text: Spread it with a finger over the joint
options.consequence: It seals the surface, and the finish will not take there.

observations.prompt: What shows that the frame is square?

options.text: The two diagonals are equal
Opposite rails are equal in length
options.why: That is true of any parallelogram, square or not.

options.text: The frame lies flat on the bench
options.why: That shows no twist. It does not show the corners are square.

numerics.prompt: A frame is {l} mm by {w} mm. What is each diagonal, to the nearest mm?

faults.scenario: Ada's frame is not square, and it has shiny patches after finishing. Here is what she did.

lines.text: She measured the diagonals only after the glue had set.
lines.why: By then it cannot be corrected.

lines.text: She left dried glue on the surfaces to be finished.
She cleaned up the inside edges before assembly.
lines.why: They are hard to reach afterwards.

lines.text: She used cramp blocks to protect the wood.

written.explainPrompt: Why does measuring the two diagonals prove that a frame is square?
written.explainGuide: A rectangle has equal diagonals. If opposite sides are equal and the diagonals are equal, every corner must be a right angle.

correct: Let samples cool in the desiccator before you handle them bare-handed.

wrong.text: Lift hot samples from the oven with a damp rag.
wrong.why: Damp cloth conducts heat fast and scalds. Use dry oven gloves.

wrong.text: Test the oven temperature by holding your hand inside.
wrong.why: Read the thermometer, not your hand.

wrong.text: Check the moisture meter by pressing its pins into your palm.
wrong.why: The pins pierce skin. Test it on a timber offcut.

distractors.why: Nothing is being sharpened.

decisions.prompt: Where do you cut the sample from?

options.text: At least 300 mm from the end of the board
options.consequence: This represents the board, because the ends dry fastest.

options.text: The very end of the board, for convenience
options.consequence: End slices are drier than the rest, so the result reads low.

options.text: Round a knot, where it is densest
options.consequence: Knots hold resin and dry differently, so the result misleads.

decisions.prompt: When do you weigh the wet sample?

options.text: Immediately after cutting
options.consequence: No moisture has escaped, so the wet mass is true.

options.text: After lunch, when the balance is free
options.consequence: It has lost moisture to the air, so the result reads low.

options.text: After a short time in the oven
options.consequence: That is already part of the drying: the wet mass is lost.

decisions.prompt: Two weighings an hour apart differ by 3 g. What do you do?

options.text: Dry it further and weigh again until the mass is constant
options.consequence: Constant mass shows all the free moisture has gone.

options.text: Take the lower figure as the dry mass and carry on working
options.consequence: It is still drying, so the moisture content comes out too low.

options.text: Average the two weighings
options.consequence: The average is not a dry mass at all.

observations.prompt: What happens to the sample's mass in the oven?

options.text: It falls, then stays constant
It falls steadily and never stops
options.why: It stops when the free moisture has gone.

options.text: It rises slowly as the wood heats
options.why: Heating adds no mass.

numerics.prompt: A sample has a wet mass of {w} g and an oven-dry mass of 200 g. What is its moisture content?

faults.scenario: Sade reports 20% moisture content for a board that actually holds 25%. Here is what she did.

written.explainPrompt: Why is moisture content worked out on the oven-dry mass, not the wet mass?
written.explainGuide: The dry mass is a fixed value for the wood, whereas the wet mass changes with the water in it, so the dry mass gives a fair base for comparing timbers.

correct: Cut away from your fingers when you pare a clean end.

wrong.text: Sand each sample hard to see the colour, without a mask.
wrong.why: Some timber dusts irritate the lungs and nose.

wrong.text: Taste the timber to help identify it.
wrong.why: Some timbers are irritant. Smell and look instead.

wrong.text: Hold the sample against your palm while cutting its end.
wrong.why: The knife can slip into your hand. Rest it on the bench.

distractors.why: Nothing is being marked out.

distractors.name: Jack plane
distractors.why: A knife gives a clean enough end.

distractors.why: Identification relies on the features listed in the key.

distractors.name: Sash cramp
distractors.why: Nothing is glued here.

decisions.prompt: Two reddish samples look alike. What do you do?

options.text: Compare grain, pores, density and smell as well

options.text: Decide on colour, which is the surest guide
options.consequence: Colour changes with age and light, so that is unreliable.

options.text: Pick the one that seems heavier

written.explainPrompt: Why does a laminated curve hold its shape better than a bent single piece?
